abstract.para: Handling I/O requests predictably is critical for deterministic performance in real-time systems. High CPU availability yields limited benefits if tasks stall while awaiting disk access.

topic.para: The Linux storage subsystem organizes process disk access into three distinct scheduling classes:

listitem.para: Grants highest priority for disk access. Requests in this class are served before any other class. Within the real-time class, priority is fine-tuned with nice levels from 0 (highest priority) to 7 (lowest priority).

warning.title: Risk of disk bandwidth starvation
warning.para: Assigning real-time I/O priorities incorrectly can deprive other system processes of disk bandwidth.
Assign real-time I/O class only to thoroughly tested critical tasks.

listitem.para: The default scheduling class for standard system processes. Priority is derived from the process CPU nice value (ranging from 0 to 7).
Processes receive disk access only when no other process requests disk I/O. Ideal for background workloads such as logging or maintenance.
